  "title": "Genealogical Depth Scoring for Recursive Web Corpus Decontamination",
  "core_problem": "Current AI-generated text detectors are binary (human vs. AI), but training corpora increasingly contain 'second-generation' synthetic text: AI outputs from models that were themselves trained on AI-generated data. This generational depth is unmeasured and unaddressed by any existing detector. Strong Model Collapse (ICLR 2025) establishes that even non-vanishing fractions (~1%) of synthetic data trigger performance collapse, yet the paper treats all synthetic data equivalently — making no distinction between Gen1 text (one model generation removed from human data) and Gen2+ text (recursively compounded). The depth-dependent contribution to collapse severity is entirely uncharacterized, and no current method can assign a generational depth score to a raw training document. Critically, recent work (arXiv:2605.01647, May 2026) demonstrates a 'Wall of Separation' where AI-AI divergence in character-distribution space is significantly smaller than human-AI divergence — making within-model generational discrimination (Gen1 vs. Gen2 from the same fine-tuned model) a harder detection problem than binary human/AI classification and motivating our use of embedding-space features that target cumulative semantic drift orthogonal to character-level surface signals.",
  "opportunity": "By April 2025, 74.2% of newly created web pages contain some AI-generated text — of which 2.5% are fully AI-generated and 71.7% are human-AI blends, where human content has been AI-revised or AI-assisted (Ahrefs, 900K pages, April 2025). These blended documents may occupy an intermediate 'Gen0.5' depth position between Gen0 and Gen1 that depth scoring can address more precisely than binary detection, and they represent the dominant contamination modality at web scale. Complete decontamination is operationally infeasible — there is not enough uncontaminated human text to replace even the fully AI-generated fraction — shifting the practical research question from 'remove all synthetic data' (impossible at web scale) to 'which synthetic documents to prioritize for removal given a fixed filtering budget.' Depth-stratified decontamination addresses this directly: if Gen2+ documents are disproportionately harmful relative to Gen1 documents, preferential removal of deeper-generation text maximizes collapse mitigation per unit of filtering effort. This claim is explicitly scoped to *severity reduction per filtering budget*, not collapse prevention, and is tested in controlled fixed-total-size depth-composition conditions that isolate the effect of contamination depth from dataset volume — making the causal evidence for the governance claim empirically clean. Strong Model Collapse (ICLR 2025) provides the urgency but not the answer — it shows synthetic data is harmful at any non-vanishing fraction but gives no guidance on whether all synthetic data is equally harmful. Crucially, the paper does not distinguish Gen1 from Gen2 synthetic data at all, leaving the depth-dependent harm gradient completely unmeasured. A depth classifier that enables tiered decontamination — or, if depth discrimination fails, definitively establishes that binary filtering suffices — constitutes a concrete empirical contribution with direct governance impact, aligned with EMNLP 2026's special theme 'New Missions for NLP Research,' which explicitly covers 'contamination, the consequences of synthetic data feedback loops, and data governance.'",
  "landscape": "Model collapse from recursive synthetic training is established (Shumailov et al., Nature 2024; Strong Model Collapse, ICLR 2025) and the limiting theory predicts collapse at any non-vanishing synthetic fraction. Mitigation via real-data accumulation (arXiv:2404.01413) or verifier-guided retraining (arXiv:2510.16657) is active. Training-side collapse prevention via Truncated Cross-Entropy loss (ForTIFAI, arXiv:2509.08972) selectively ignores high-confidence tokens during training to filter synthetic artifacts — a complementary but orthogonal approach to our upstream corpus-level depth detection: ForTIFAI does not classify documents by generational depth and does not operate pre-training. The closest upstream related work, 'Machine-generated text detection prevents language model collapse' (arXiv:2502.15654, Drayson, Yilmaz, Lampos, UCL, Feb 2025), directly bridges AI-text detection and collapse prevention: it trains encoder-only binary classifiers (evaluating RoBERTa, DeBERTa-v3, and ModernBERT) to distinguish human from AI-generated text, then applies importance resampling — weighting each training document by (1-q(x))^b where q(x) is the classifier's AI-probability score — to up-weight likely human content during recursive training. Experiments across GPT-2 and SmolLM2 (124M–1.7B parameters) demonstrate that binary-classifier-guided resampling prevents collapse and even improves over training on purely human data. Critically, arXiv:2502.15654 treats all AI-generated text as equivalent regardless of generational provenance: importance weights depend only on a single binary human/AI probability, with no distinction between Gen1 text (one fine-tuning cycle removed from human data) and Gen2+ text (recursively compounded). Our work directly addresses this gap: if depth-stratified resampling weights — proportional to estimated generational distance from Gen0 — yield greater collapse-severity reduction per resampled document than flat binary weights, preferential down-weighting of Gen2+ text constitutes a principled improvement over arXiv:2502.15654's strategy under budget-constrained filtering. The dual null-hypothesis design explicitly covers the scenario where depth discrimination fails (AUC < 0.65), in which case our results empirically validate arXiv:2502.15654's implicit assumption that generational depth is irrelevant and binary resampling is sufficient — a governance finding with direct practical value. A mathematical framework for how recursive publication compresses text through drift and selection is developed in arXiv:2604.08554 but does not propose a depth classifier. The framework is derived for variable-order n-gram agents and does not address transformer fine-tuning; extension to neural models is an open theoretical question that our experiments probe empirically. AI-generated text detection (arXiv:2303.11156, arXiv:2509.18880) addresses binary classification and reaches AUC ~0.85-0.90 for Gen1 text, uniformly treating all AI-generated text as equivalent regardless of generational provenance. Embedding-based representations show intrinsic separability between AI-generated and human text in compressed embedding spaces (arXiv:2408.10437), motivating our use of embedding-space distance features alongside surface-level signals. 'Understanding Transformers via N-gram Statistics' (arXiv:2407.12034, NeurIPS 2024) provides empirical motivation for applying n-gram-derived theoretical predictions to transformer fine-tuning: transformer next-token predictions agree with n-gram rulesets for 68–79% of distributions across TinyStories and Wikipedia, suggesting transformer distributional behavior closely approximates n-gram statistics at the local prediction level — supporting our hypothesis that the monotonic drift prediction of arXiv:2604.08554 (derived for n-gram agents) extends to transformer fine-tuning at the distributional level, with our experiments constituting a direct empirical test of this generalization. 'Beyond Perplexity: Character Distribution Signatures and the MDTA Benchmark for AI Text Detection' (arXiv:2605.01647, May 2026) introduces the Letter Distribution Score (LD-Score) and establishes a 'Wall of Separation' where human-AI divergence significantly exceeds AI-AI divergence in character-distribution space — with the direct implication that within-model generational divergence (Gen1 vs. Gen2 from the same fine-tuned 0.6B model) is smaller still than cross-model AI-AI divergence. This finding validates our architectural choice to prioritize embedding-space features over character-distribution proxies: our mean cosine distance from Gen0 centroid and within-document embedding variance operate in a representation space where cumulative semantic drift — predicted to accumulate monotonically by arXiv:2604.08554's recursive drift-selection framework — may remain detectable even when surface and character-level signals converge. The pre-specified AUC threshold (0.65) and dual null-hypothesis pivot design explicitly account for the scenario where depth discrimination fails at the document level despite embedding-space features. No paper in the contamination detection surveys (arXiv:2502.14425, arXiv:2406.04244) addresses generation depth as a variable. The closest concurrent work — 'Beyond Surface-Level Similarity: Hierarchical Contamination Detection for Synthetic Training Data in Foundation Models' (arXiv:2511.17602, Nov 2025) — asks whether synthetic data overlaps with evaluation benchmarks, not how many generative cycles deep a document is; generational ancestry is orthogonal to benchmark overlap. 'Training Data Provenance Verification: Did Your Model Use Synthetic Data from My Generative Model for Training?' (TrainProVe, CVPR 2025, arXiv:2503.09122) achieves >99% accuracy verifying which text-to-image model generated a given image, using model access and generalization error bounds — differentiation is sharp: TrainProVe operates in the image domain and requires model weights access, while our method operates on raw text documents with no model access, enabling upstream corpus-level pre-filtering. Both address data governance but via entirely complementary mechanisms. 'A Closer Look at Model Collapse' (arXiv:2509.16499, NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight) identifies a generalization-to-memorization transition but studies diffusion models and does not distinguish depth levels in training data.",
  "approach": "We build a controlled genealogical corpus by running a 2-step recursive train-generate loop with Qwen3-0.6B (the smallest Qwen3 model, chosen to minimize sequential compute cost while still exhibiting measurable distributional drift per generation), producing text with verified depth labels Gen0 (human, sourced from FineWeb-Edu and C4), Gen1, and Gen2, yielding ~200K labeled documents per depth level across diverse domains. We disable Qwen3-0.6B thinking mode during all generative steps via the hard switch `enable_thinking=False` in `tokenizer.apply_chat_template`, rather than the soft `/no_think` instruction tag — because GitHub discussion QwenLM/Qwen3 #1329 documents that the 0.6B model lacks sufficient instruction-following capacity to reliably honor `/no_think` when placed in the system prompt, and silent failure would inject `<think>…</think>` reasoning traces into Gen1/Gen2 documents that are absent from Gen0 human text, making depth levels trivially separable by token-level artifacts rather than genuine semantic drift and invalidating the AUC signal. The `enable_thinking=False` hard switch operates at the tokenizer template level and does not depend on the model's instruction-following capacity. As a final post-hoc verification, every generated document is scanned for `<think>` tokens and discarded if any are found, before corpus inclusion.

Limiting to Gen0/Gen1/Gen2 compresses the sequential corpus construction bottleneck to approximately 2 wallclock days: Qwen3-0.6B fine-tuning on a 200K-document sample runs in ~4-6 GPU hours on A100, and generation of 200K new documents runs in ~6-8 GPU hours, for ~12-14 GPU hours per generational step. The hard sequential dependency spans only 2 steps.

We train a DeBERTa-v3-large ordinal regression classifier jointly on raw text and depth-diagnostic features spanning two categories: (a) surface-level signals — per-token surprisal variance (burstiness), lexical diversity decay (MTLD and type-token ratio), and n-gram entropy compression ratio; and (b) embedding-space signals — (i) mean cosine distance of within-document window embeddings from the pre-computed Gen0 centroid (capturing average depth of embedding drift from human text), and (ii) variance of per-window cosine distances from the Gen0 centroid within the document (capturing within-document heterogeneity of embedding drift). Both embedding features are computed from non-overlapping 128-token window embeddings produced by sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2; feature (i) measures central tendency and feature (ii) measures distributional spread — distinct geometric properties: a Gen2 document may exhibit both higher mean distance from Gen0 and more heterogeneous window-level drift than a Gen1 document, as cumulative generational compression produces uneven semantic displacement within a document. We integrate these five scalar depth-diagnostic features by concatenating them to the DeBERTa-v3-large CLS token representation (1024-dim), then training an ordinal regression head over this joint 1029-dim representation; the Gen0 embedding centroid is precomputed offline from a held-out Gen0 reference set of 10K documents using sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and is not updated during classifier training.

Embedding-space features are specifically motivated by the 'Wall of Separation' established in arXiv:2605.01647 (May 2026): AI-AI character-distribution divergence is significantly smaller than human-AI divergence, and within-model generational divergence (Gen1→Gen2 from the same fine-tuned 0.6B model) is smaller still. Surface-level and character-distribution signals are therefore unlikely to reliably discriminate depth levels in this setting; our mean cosine distance from Gen0 centroid and within-document embedding variance instead target cumulative semantic drift that arXiv:2604.08554's recursive drift-selection framework predicts to accumulate monotonically across generations even when character distributions plateau — providing detection signal orthogonal to surface proxies. The argument is: our embedding-space features target cumulative semantic drift that persists even when surface divergence converges, consistent with the monotonic drift predicted by arXiv:2604.08554 — with the explicit caveat that arXiv:2604.08554 derives this prediction for variable-order n-gram agents, not transformer fine-tuning. We hypothesize the generalization holds because transformer next-token distributions closely approximate n-gram statistics at the local prediction level (arXiv:2407.12034, NeurIPS 2024, reports 68–79% agreement between transformer predictions and n-gram rulesets across two corpora), suggesting transformer fine-tuning implicitly performs distributional compression analogous to n-gram compression, for which cumulative drift is expected to accumulate monotonically. Our classifier and collapse experiments directly test whether this hypothesized generalization from n-gram theory to transformer practice holds empirically.

Central technical risk and dual null-hypothesis design: We pre-specify two complementary pre-registered outcome scenarios to ensure a definitive, interpretable empirical finding under all classifier and collapse experiment outcomes. (Primary null) If the ordinal classifier falls below AUC 0.65 on Gen1/Gen2 discrimination, the finding is publishable: depth beyond Gen1 is linguistically indistinguishable at the document level using current text-level and embedding-level methods, implying binary filtering suffices — consistent with the implicit assumption of arXiv:2502.15654. In this case, the collapse validation experiments automatically pivot to directly comparing binary (Gen0-only) filtering against depth-stratified filtering at fixed corpus size. (Secondary null) If the classifier achieves AUC ≥ 0.65 but collapse validation shows statistically indistinguishable held-out perplexity between conditions (b) (100K Gen0 + 100K Gen1) and (c) (67K Gen0 + 67K Gen1 + 66K Gen2) at fixed total corpus size (paired t-test, α = 0.05, across 3 random seeds), we report this as a distinct secondary null outcome: depth detection is feasible but equal-fraction Gen2 contamination causes no additional collapse-severity beyond equal-fraction Gen1 contamination at GPT-2 scale — the marginal harm-per-generation curve is flat at this model size, binary filtering is sufficient for practical governance at small scales, and preferential Gen2 removal yields no measurable advantage at this scale. This finding has direct governance implications while leaving open whether depth stratification provides additional value at larger model scales, explicitly reserved as future work. All four logical combinations of (AUC pass/fail) × (collapse severity parity/non-parity) produce pre-specified, interpretable empirical contributions with distinct governance implications.

The trained classifier is applied zero-shot to real FineWeb and C4 slices to estimate depth-distribution statistics of existing pretraining corpora. Collapse validation uses a GPT-2-scale LM fine-tuned on three fixed-total-size depth-composition conditions (200K training documents each), following the controlled-composition standard of Strong Model Collapse (ICLR 2025): (a) Gen0-only: 200K Gen0; (b) Gen0+Gen1: 100K Gen0 + 100K Gen1; (c) Gen0+Gen1+Gen2: 67K Gen0 + 67K Gen1 + 66K Gen2. These corpora are constructed by subsampling from the already-generated 200K-document pools at each depth level, requiring no additional generation compute. Fixing total corpus size at 200K across all three conditions isolates the causal effect of depth composition from dataset volume: any observed collapse severity difference between conditions reflects contamination depth, not training set size — making the central governance claim ('Gen2 contamination is more harmful per document than Gen1 at equal contamination rate') empirically defensible. Collapse severity is tracked via held-out human-text perplexity and output tail entropy across multiple recursive training generations, explicitly scoped to measuring *severity as a function of depth composition at fixed scale* rather than collapse prevention — consistent with Strong Model Collapse's any-fraction harm finding. GenDepth-Bench is scoped to 2 model families: Qwen3-0.6B (primary) and Llama-3.2-1B (secondary, run through the same recursive loop to test cross-model generalizability of depth signals, explicitly optional — executed only if compute budget permits; see resource estimate). Coverage of 5+ model families is explicitly reserved as future work.

16-Day Critical Path (EMNLP 2026 ARR deadline May 25, 2026; today May 9, 2026):
— Days 1-2: Environment setup; sample 200K Gen0 docs from FineWeb-Edu/C4; prepare evaluation suite and draft intro/related-work sections.
— Days 2-3 (sequential bottleneck step 1): Fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B on Gen0 (~4-6h GPU); generate 200K Gen1 documents (~6-8h GPU) with `enable_thinking=False` hard switch and post-hoc `<think>` token scan.
— Days 3-4 (sequential bottleneck step 2): Fine-tune Qwen3-0.6B-v2 on Gen1 (~4-6h GPU); generate 200K Gen2 documents (~6-8h GPU) with same thinking-mode controls.
— Days 3-8 (PARALLEL TRACK A): DeBERTa-v3-large ordinal training begins with Gen0+Gen1 data at Day 3; adds Gen2 data when available at Day 5; ablations over surface vs. embedding feature subsets.
— Days 5-10 (PARALLEL TRACK B): GPT-2-scale collapse experiments begin at Day 5 with fixed-size conditions (a) Gen0-only: 200K Gen0 and (b) Gen0+Gen1: 100K Gen0+100K Gen1 (subsampled from existing pools); add condition (c) Gen0+Gen1+Gen2: 67K each at Day 6 when Gen2 corpus is available. Llama-3.2-1B recursive corpus generation runs in parallel if compute budget is below 160h H100-equivalent at Day 5.
— Days 7-9: Full classifier evaluation; if Gen1/Gen2 AUC < 0.65, activate primary null-hypothesis binary filtering comparison experiments; if AUC ≥ 0.65 but collapse severity parity detected between conditions (b) and (c), record secondary null outcome and report governance implications.
— Days 9-10: Zero-shot depth scoring on real FineWeb/C4 slices.
— Days 10-12: Feature importance ablations; cross-model generalizability check on Llama-3.2-1B-generated corpus (if optional Llama recursive corpus was generated).
— Days 12-16: Analysis, writing, revision, and submission.",

  "description": "As web corpora become saturated with AI-generated content (74.2% of new web pages contain some AI text by April 2025, of which 2.5% are fully AI-generated and 71.7% are human-AI blends; Ahrefs, 900K pages), complete decontamination is operationally infeasible, shifting the question to: which synthetic documents cause the most harm and should be removed first? These five scalar features are concatenated to the DeBERTa-v3-large CLS token representation (1024-dim) and passed to an ordinal regression head trained over the joint 1029-dim representation; the Gen0 centroid is precomputed offline and not updated during training.
